tagline: Dunes, desert elephants, and endless sky
overview:
Namibia occupies Africa's southwest corner, where the Namib Desert, probably the oldest desert on Earth, runs the entire length of the Atlantic coast. The country is bigger than Texas but one of the emptiest places on the planet: only about 2.6 million people live there, roughly three for every square kilometer.

Windhoek, the capital, stands on a highland plateau in the middle of the country. English is the official language, while Afrikaans and German are still widely spoken from colonial days, and most families use a language such as Oshiwambo, Herero, Khoekhoe, Kwangali, Lozi, Ndonga, or Tswana at home. Namibia is a republic with an elected president, independent only since 1990, which makes it one of Africa's youngest nations.

Mining for diamonds and uranium, cattle and sheep ranching, fishing the cold Atlantic, and visitors drawn to the dunes and game parks keep the country running.
landAndNature: Two deserts bracket Namibia: the Namib along the coast, where the dunes of Sossusvlei rise more than 300 meters and glow orange at sunrise, and the Kalahari in the east. Between them lies a dry central plateau of thornbush and rocky hills. The cold Benguela Current keeps the coast foggy and almost rainless, and that fog is the only water for beetles that stand on their heads to let droplets run into their mouths. Etosha National Park surrounds a vast salt pan where elephants, black rhinos, lions, and springbok crowd the waterholes. Desert-adapted elephants and lions survive in the dry northwest, and Cape fur seals pack the beaches by the tens of thousands.
peopleAndCulture: The largest group is the Ovambo, alongside Herero, Damara, Nama, Kavango, Himba, San, and Afrikaner communities among many others. Herero women wear long Victorian-style dresses and horn-shaped headdresses, while Himba people in the northwest coat their skin and hair with a red mixture of ochre and butterfat. Most Namibians are Christian. Meals range from oshifima, a stiff millet porridge, to biltong, dried spiced meat, with German-influenced bakeries and sausages in Windhoek and Swakopmund. Soccer and rugby draw crowds, and the sprinter Frankie Fredericks won four Olympic silver medals in the 1990s. Independence Day on March 21 fills the streets with parades, and village conservancies manage wildlife and share the income from tourism.
history: San hunter-gatherers have lived in this land for tens of thousands of years, leaving rock engravings at Twyfelfontein; Bantu-speaking herders and farmers arrived later. Germany claimed the territory as German South West Africa in 1884. When the Herero and Nama peoples rose up against colonial land seizures in 1904, German forces drove them into the desert and into camps, killing the great majority of both peoples, a genocide that Germany formally acknowledged in 2021. After World War I South Africa took over and later imposed its apartheid racial laws. The SWAPO movement fought a long independence war from 1966, and Namibia finally became independent on March 21, 1990, with Sam Nujoma as its first president.
funFacts: Namibia was among the first countries in the world to write protection of the environment into its constitution.
The Skeleton Coast takes its name from the shipwrecks and whale bones left along its fog-bound beaches.
The Fish River Canyon is about 160 kilometers long and up to 550 meters deep, often called the second largest canyon on Earth.
The NamibRand Reserve has some of the darkest night skies anywhere and is protected as an international dark sky reserve.
In Deadvlei, camel thorn trees that died around 900 years ago still stand on a white clay pan, too dry to rot away.
